metadata.narrative: I am a pre-school teacher for ages 3-4. Please provide me a detailed report on a strategy for the following situation: One student doesn't want to share and always gets into tantrums when I tell them about the sharing rules. During these tantrums, they hurt other students. They bargain with ice cream, saying they will stop if they get some. I tried to follow a gentle, preventative approach, but it doesn't work for this student.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Since your gentle, preventative-only approach is not enough for this particular child, the strongest path is to move toward an individualized, structured plan built around three pillars: teaching concrete sharing skills, changing how you respond during tantrums and aggression, and eliminating the ice-cream bargaining pattern through consistent limits.

Start by treating this as a specific behavior to investigate rather than a generic "won't share" problem, using a simple observation diary that records what happens right before the tantrum, how intense and long it is, and what the child seems to get or avoid from it each time.

Early-childhood specialists recommend a five-step Positive Behaviour Management Plan for persistent challenging behaviors: list and prioritize the specific behaviors, form a no-blame hypothesis about why each happens, build a plan with environmental adjustments and natural or logical consequences, anticipate barriers, and then trial and review the plan regularly rather than assuming one approach will work immediately.

This framework notes that hitting, biting, snatching, and tantrums generally serve one of three functions—getting something, avoiding something, or meeting an unmet sensory or emotional need—so identifying which function drives this child's behavior should guide your specific supports.
On the sharing skill itself, remember that preschoolers do not yet grasp sharing the way adults do, so the goal is to teach concrete turn-taking tools rather than repeating a rule.

A useful phrase to teach is "Can I have that when you're finished?", which lets a child state a need without grabbing while reassuring the peer their turn will come, defusing disputes that would otherwise end in grabbing.

Stopwatch or visual timer games, where a toy passes back and forth on a set schedule, help children learn that giving something up is not permanent, and pairing this with descriptive praise about how the other child felt reinforces the behavior more than generic praise.
Stocking duplicate copies of popular toys and practicing calming and turn-taking skills proactively remains a core preventative step, even though it is clearly not sufficient alone for this child.

When a dispute is actively happening, use a structured conflict-resolution sequence rather than only restating the sharing rule: calmly ask both children what happened without judgment, invite them to brainstorm solutions, and help them choose and try one together, repeating the agreed plan back to both.

Broader guidance adds that teachers should stay alert to crowding or scarce resources that predict conflict, pause to get calm before intervening, and use open-ended questioning rather than directing children to a predetermined "fair" outcome, since directing removes children's own practice of communication and perspective-taking.
Because this child's tantrums include hurting others, the response needs a distinct, safety-first script layered on top of the sharing conversation.

When aggression occurs, separate the children first and check on the child who was hurt, then calmly and firmly state "No hitting, hitting hurts," avoiding yelling or physical punishment, which can increase tantrum severity and teaches that aggression is acceptable when angry.

After everyone is calm, briefly discuss the incident and role-play an alternative response such as saying "stop," walking away, or telling an adult, since children need practice with replacement behaviors, not just a "no."
A concrete replacement behavior, such as teaching the child to clap their hands or use a specific phrase when the urge to grab or hit rises, gives them a physical outlet that does not hurt anyone.

Clinical guidance frames the tantrum moment with the acronym R.I.D.D.—remain calm, ignore the tantrum itself, distract or redirect, and do meet genuine safety needs without giving in to demands—paired with C.A.L.M. for prevention: communicate feelings, attend to needs proactively, let the child share feelings and have appropriate choices, and maintain predictable routines.
That same source states explicitly that giving in to demands during a tantrum may reinforce the undesired behavior, which is the exact mechanism behind the ice-cream bargaining you're seeing.
The ice-cream negotiation deserves its own targeted response because it is a textbook case of bribery reinforcing tantrums rather than reducing them.

Rewards are set up in advance for good behavior, while bribery is offered mid-tantrum, and if a child asks "what will you give me if I stop," that is bribery by definition; giving in teaches that misbehavior produces the treat while calm behavior produces nothing.

Reinforcement must be planned before the behavior occurs, whereas bribing mid-tantrum instead reinforces the tantrum itself, and repeated bribery escalates as children learn to negotiate for bigger rewards.

The recommended alternative is extinction: stop providing the attention, item, or escape the tantrum has been earning, while separately setting up a reinforcement system in advance, such as a small sticker or token earned for using words or waiting for a turn, gradually faded and paired with genuine praise.

A broader behavior-change model confirms this order: verify the child's basic needs are met, adjust the environment to reduce triggers, use positive reinforcement for the wanted behavior, teach an alternate behavior, and use extinction sparingly since removing an established reinforcer can temporarily intensify behavior before it improves.

Practically, tell the child before any sharing situation what they will earn for handling it well, and during an actual tantrum offer no treats, no extended negotiation, and no early exit from the sharing expectation, while still ensuring safety.
For non-aggressive protest that is not hurting anyone, calmly ignoring it while reserving active intervention specifically for aggressive acts keeps your response proportionate and consistent.

Separating commentary on the behavior from feelings about the child, saying "I don't like seeing you grab the toy" rather than labeling the child bad, keeps the relationship intact, and temporarily removing shared materials until the group can play cooperatively again functions as a natural consequence tied directly to the behavior.

Because this pattern has persisted despite gentle prevention, build an individualized plan and share it with the family so home and school use the same language and consequences, since inconsistency between settings is a recognized driver of persistent challenging behavior.

Finally, treat the plan as provisional: keep the behavior diary running and adjust the hypothesis if a few weeks of consistent implementation show no improvement, rather than assuming the first version is final.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

answer.text: Since your gentle, preventative-only approach is not enough for this particular child, the strongest path is to move toward an individualized, structured plan built around three pillars: teaching concrete sharing skills, changing how you respond during tantrums and aggression, and eliminating the ice-cream bargaining pattern through consistent limits.

Start by treating this as a specific behavior to investigate rather than a generic "won't share" problem, using a simple observation diary that records what happens right before the tantrum, how intense and long it is, and what the child seems to get or avoid from it each time.

Early-childhood specialists recommend a five-step Positive Behaviour Management Plan for persistent challenging behaviors: list and prioritize the specific behaviors, form a no-blame hypothesis about why each happens, build a plan with environmental adjustments and natural or logical consequences, anticipate barriers, and then trial and review the plan regularly rather than assuming one approach will work immediately.

This framework notes that hitting, biting, snatching, and tantrums generally serve one of three functions—getting something, avoiding something, or meeting an unmet sensory or emotional need—so identifying which function drives this child's behavior should guide your specific supports.
On the sharing skill itself, remember that preschoolers do not yet grasp sharing the way adults do, so the goal is to teach concrete turn-taking tools rather than repeating a rule.

A useful phrase to teach is "Can I have that when you're finished?", which lets a child state a need without grabbing while reassuring the peer their turn will come, defusing disputes that would otherwise end in grabbing.

Stopwatch or visual timer games, where a toy passes back and forth on a set schedule, help children learn that giving something up is not permanent, and pairing this with descriptive praise about how the other child felt reinforces the behavior more than generic praise.
Stocking duplicate copies of popular toys and practicing calming and turn-taking skills proactively remains a core preventative step, even though it is clearly not sufficient alone for this child.

When a dispute is actively happening, use a structured conflict-resolution sequence rather than only restating the sharing rule: calmly ask both children what happened without judgment, invite them to brainstorm solutions, and help them choose and try one together, repeating the agreed plan back to both.

Broader guidance adds that teachers should stay alert to crowding or scarce resources that predict conflict, pause to get calm before intervening, and use open-ended questioning rather than directing children to a predetermined "fair" outcome, since directing removes children's own practice of communication and perspective-taking.
Because this child's tantrums include hurting others, the response needs a distinct, safety-first script layered on top of the sharing conversation.

When aggression occurs, separate the children first and check on the child who was hurt, then calmly and firmly state "No hitting, hitting hurts," avoiding yelling or physical punishment, which can increase tantrum severity and teaches that aggression is acceptable when angry.

After everyone is calm, briefly discuss the incident and role-play an alternative response such as saying "stop," walking away, or telling an adult, since children need practice with replacement behaviors, not just a "no."
A concrete replacement behavior, such as teaching the child to clap their hands or use a specific phrase when the urge to grab or hit rises, gives them a physical outlet that does not hurt anyone.

Clinical guidance frames the tantrum moment with the acronym R.I.D.D.—remain calm, ignore the tantrum itself, distract or redirect, and do meet genuine safety needs without giving in to demands—paired with C.A.L.M. for prevention: communicate feelings, attend to needs proactively, let the child share feelings and have appropriate choices, and maintain predictable routines.
That same source states explicitly that giving in to demands during a tantrum may reinforce the undesired behavior, which is the exact mechanism behind the ice-cream bargaining you're seeing.
The ice-cream negotiation deserves its own targeted response because it is a textbook case of bribery reinforcing tantrums rather than reducing them.

Rewards are set up in advance for good behavior, while bribery is offered mid-tantrum, and if a child asks "what will you give me if I stop," that is bribery by definition; giving in teaches that misbehavior produces the treat while calm behavior produces nothing.

Reinforcement must be planned before the behavior occurs, whereas bribing mid-tantrum instead reinforces the tantrum itself, and repeated bribery escalates as children learn to negotiate for bigger rewards.

The recommended alternative is extinction: stop providing the attention, item, or escape the tantrum has been earning, while separately setting up a reinforcement system in advance, such as a small sticker or token earned for using words or waiting for a turn, gradually faded and paired with genuine praise.

A broader behavior-change model confirms this order: verify the child's basic needs are met, adjust the environment to reduce triggers, use positive reinforcement for the wanted behavior, teach an alternate behavior, and use extinction sparingly since removing an established reinforcer can temporarily intensify behavior before it improves.

Practically, tell the child before any sharing situation what they will earn for handling it well, and during an actual tantrum offer no treats, no extended negotiation, and no early exit from the sharing expectation, while still ensuring safety.
For non-aggressive protest that is not hurting anyone, calmly ignoring it while reserving active intervention specifically for aggressive acts keeps your response proportionate and consistent.

Separating commentary on the behavior from feelings about the child, saying "I don't like seeing you grab the toy" rather than labeling the child bad, keeps the relationship intact, and temporarily removing shared materials until the group can play cooperatively again functions as a natural consequence tied directly to the behavior.

Because this pattern has persisted despite gentle prevention, build an individualized plan and share it with the family so home and school use the same language and consequences, since inconsistency between settings is a recognized driver of persistent challenging behavior.

Finally, treat the plan as provisional: keep the behavior diary running and adjust the hypothesis if a few weeks of consistent implementation show no improvement, rather than assuming the first version is final.
